mcqs.question: An object store advertises 11 nines of durability but has a brief availability dip during a failover. Is this a contradiction?
options: Yes — durability and availability mean the same thing, so one can't hold while the other drops
No — durability is about whether the data still exists somewhere, while availability is about whether it can be read right now; a system can be extremely durable while briefly unavailable
No, because 11 nines durability only applies to reads, not to failover events
Yes — any availability dip automatically means data was permanently lost
mcqs.explanation: Durability and availability are genuinely separate guarantees: durability asks whether the bytes still exist somewhere (even offline or mid-failover), availability asks whether you can retrieve them at this exact moment. A brief read failure during failover doesn't imply data loss. The other options conflate the two or misapply the durability figure.

mcqs.question: Why might an object store use both replication and erasure coding, rather than picking just one for everything?
options: Erasure coding is strictly better in every respect, so replication is only kept for legacy reasons
Replication is required by law for certain object types
The two techniques must always be used together on every object for correctness
Replication suits hot, frequently-read data where simplicity and low CPU cost matter; erasure coding suits the bulk of cold, rarely-accessed data where storage cost dominates
mcqs.explanation: The two techniques trade differently: replication is cheap on CPU and fast to read but costly in storage, erasure coding is the reverse. Tiering by access pattern — replication for hot data, erasure coding for cold bulk data — captures the benefit of each. There's no legal mandate and no requirement to combine both on every object.

mcqs.question: At 100 billion objects, why does the metadata service, not the storage nodes, become the harder scaling problem?
options: Storage nodes scale by simply adding more disks/nodes for capacity, while every single put/get call touches the metadata service, making its lookup index itself a distributed-database-scale challenge
Storage nodes cannot be added incrementally past a fixed limit
Metadata records are actually larger in size than the objects they describe
The metadata service only needs to handle a small fraction of total request volume
mcqs.explanation: Raw storage capacity scales close to linearly by adding nodes; the metadata service instead sees every single operation and must serve key lookups at full request volume across a keyspace of billions of entries — a much harder scaling problem. Storage nodes aren't capacity-limited in this way, metadata records are tiny compared to objects, and the metadata service sees the full request volume, not a small fraction.
